title: FAR U2·W1 — Investments: Debt & Equity Securities, Equity Method (CPA Core)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — where does the gain go?

The single most-tested idea in FAR investments is where an unrealized gain lands — net income or other comprehensive income — and that depends entirely on classification. The same $15,000 gain hits earnings under one classification and bypasses earnings under another. This unit sorts debt securities, equity securities, and significant-influence investments.

Debt securities — three classifications

  • Held-to-maturity (HTM) — intent and ability to hold to maturity. Reported at amortized cost; unrealized changes are not recognized.
  • Trading — bought to sell short-term. Reported at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in net income.
  • Available-for-sale (AFS) — the default for debt not in the other two. Reported at fair value with unrealized gains/losses in other comprehensive income (OCI) until sold.

Illustrative: a debt security cost $100,000 and is worth $115,000 at year-end. As trading, the $15,000 unrealized gain goes to net income. As AFS, the same $15,000 goes to OCI. As HTM, no gain is recognized — it stays at amortized cost.

Equity securities

For equity investments without significant influence, the rule is simpler: report at fair value with changes in net income (there is no AFS treatment for equity securities under current GAAP). So an equity security held at fair value runs its unrealized gains and losses through earnings each period. A narrow practicability exception lets an entity measure an equity security without a readily determinable fair value at cost less impairment, adjusted for observable price changes.

Significant influence — the equity method

When an investor owns roughly 20% to 50% of the voting stock (presumed significant influence), it uses the equity method, not fair value. The investment is recorded at cost and then:

  • increased by the investor's share of investee net income (and decreased by its share of losses), and
  • decreased by dividends received (dividends are a return of investment, not income).

Illustrative: buy 30% for $300,000. The investee earns $200,000 → add 30% × $200,000 = $60,000 to the investment and to equity-method income. The investee pays $50,000 of dividends → reduce the investment by 30% × $50,000 = $15,000. Ending investment = $300,000 + $60,000 − $15,000 = $345,000. Above 50% ownership, the investor consolidates instead (the intercompany-elimination logic from CMA month 7).

Impairment and credit losses

HTM debt securities follow the CECL model (ASC 326): the investor records an allowance for expected credit losses through net income and presents the security net of that allowance, recognizing expected losses up front rather than waiting for a loss event. AFS debt securities use a separate model: when fair value is below amortized cost and the shortfall is credit-related, the investor recognizes an allowance for credit losses in net income — capped at the difference between fair value and amortized cost — while any non-credit portion of the decline stays in OCI. If the entity intends to sell, or will more likely than not be required to sell before recovery, it writes the security all the way down to fair value through earnings. Equity securities need no OCI-impairment model because their changes already run through net income; the lone exception is the practicability-election equity security carried at cost, which is assessed qualitatively and written down to fair value through earnings when impaired.

Selling a security and the reclassification adjustment

When an AFS debt security is sold, the cumulative unrealized gain or loss sitting in accumulated OCI is removed and the realized gain or loss recognized in net income — a reclassification adjustment. If the AFS security that rose to $115,000 is later sold, the amount previously parked in OCI is reclassified out of OCI and into earnings so comprehensive income is not double-counted. Trading securities need no such adjustment because their gains already hit earnings each period. This OCI-recycling mechanic is a favorite trap: an AFS gain is recognized in earnings only when realized, while the periodic mark waits in OCI in the interim.

Reclassifications between categories

Transfers among HTM, AFS, and trading are recorded at fair value on the transfer date, and the unrealized gain’s treatment depends on direction. Transferring into trading recognizes the unrealized gain immediately in net income; transferring out of trading leaves the already-recognized gain in income. Moving debt from HTM to AFS books the unrealized gain in OCI; from AFS to HTM, the existing OCI amount is amortized over the remaining life. Frequent sales or transfers out of HTM can taint the whole HTM portfolio and force reclassification to AFS — which is why HTM demands genuine positive intent and ability to hold to maturity.

Equity-method nuances the exam tests

Beyond add-income / subtract-dividends, the equity method carries subtleties. At acquisition, any excess of cost over the investor’s share of the investee’s book value is a basis difference allocated to identifiable assets (then depreciated or amortized against equity-method income), with the remainder treated as equity-method goodwill (not amortized). The investor also eliminates its share of intra-entity profits on transactions with the investee until realized. If the investee reports losses, the investor records its share only down to a zero investment balance (plus any loans or guarantees), then suspends further losses until the investee returns to profit. An investor may instead elect the fair value option — an irrevocable, instrument-by-instrument choice — carrying the investment at fair value through earnings.

Worked basis difference: pay $300,000 for 30% when 30% of book value is $250,000. Of the $50,000 excess, say $30,000 relates to undervalued equipment with a 10-year life and $20,000 is goodwill. The investor amortizes $3,000 per year ($30,000 ÷ 10) against equity-method income while leaving the $20,000 goodwill intact — so first-year equity income of $60,000 becomes $57,000 after the basis-difference amortization.

A worked AFS year in journal entries

Trace one AFS debt security through a full cycle. Buy at $100,000: debit AFS investment $100,000, credit cash. At year-end fair value $115,000: debit the fair-value adjustment $15,000 and credit unrealized gain — OCI $15,000, so the balance sheet shows $115,000 with $15,000 in accumulated OCI. Next year fair value slips to $108,000 before sale: debit unrealized holding loss — OCI $7,000, credit the adjustment $7,000, leaving $8,000 in accumulated OCI. On sale at $108,000: derecognize the carrying amount, remove the $8,000 accumulated OCI, and recognize a realized gain in net income equal to proceeds minus original cost ($108,000 − $100,000 = $8,000). The cumulative effect on comprehensive income over the holding period equals the single $8,000 economic gain — OCI merely timed it.

IFRS contrast

IFRS 9 classifies financial assets by a business-model test and a cash-flow characteristics (SPPI) test rather than by management-intent labels. Debt instruments fall into amortized cost (held to collect contractual cash flows that are solely principal and interest), fair value through OCI (held to collect and sell), or fair value through profit or loss (everything else). For equity investments not held for trading, IFRS permits an irrevocable election to present fair-value changes in OCI — but, unlike US GAAP debt-AFS, those amounts are never recycled to profit or loss on sale. IFRS applies a single expected-credit-loss model across debt instruments, whereas US GAAP splits CECL (HTM) from the AFS allowance approach. The equity method exists under both frameworks at significant influence.

CMA bridge

CMA month 7 covered fair value (ASC 820) and intercompany eliminations; FAR investments add the classification rules that decide whether a fair-value change hits net income or OCI, and the equity method that bridges between fair-value accounting and full consolidation.

Practice and recap

  1. Classify a debt security as HTM (amortized cost), trading (FV → NI), or AFS (FV → OCI).
  2. Carry equity securities at fair value through net income (no AFS for equity).
  3. Apply the equity method at 20–50%: add share of income, subtract dividends.
  4. Consolidate above 50%.

Recap: classification decides the destination — a $15,000 unrealized gain is net income if trading, OCI if AFS, and unrecognized if HTM. At 30% ownership the equity method carries the investment to $345,000 after adding $60,000 of income and subtracting $15,000 of dividends.

questions.q: A held-to-maturity debt security is reported at:
questions.explain: HTM securities are carried at amortized cost.

questions.q: An equity security with no significant influence is generally measured at:
questions.explain: Equity securities are carried at fair value with changes in net income; there is no AFS category for equity.

questions.explain: 20–50% with significant influence uses the equity method.

questions.q: Under the equity method, a 30% investor whose investee earns $200,000 records:
choices: $60,000 income and a $60,000 increase in the investment
questions.explain: Add the investor's 30% share ($60,000) to both income and the investment carrying amount.

questions.q: Under the equity method, dividends received from the investee:
questions.explain: Dividends are a return of investment and reduce the investment balance, not income.
